title: Big bang, small change
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: theartofaskingquestions.com (The Art of Asking Questions), October 18, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli presents the argument of organisational development specialist Mark Eddleston, author of The Pigeon Test: Why Change Fails, that big-bang transformation programmes keep failing because organisations are complex adaptive systems rather than machines. He explains Samir Rihani's catapult-and-pigeon illustration: a ball fired from a catapult lands predictably, whereas a pigeon responds to its surroundings and makes its own choices. A motorway jam with no cause shows how the whole behaves differently from its parts. Big-bang change breaks the pattern that holds an organisation together while it adapts, and cannot choose the pattern that forms next, so people stop learning and start bracing. The article contrasts this with the pandemic's shift to remote work, a constraint imposed from outside with details left to the people doing the work, and notes that return-to-office mandates then met falling satisfaction without financial gain. It explains why linear transformation keeps selling, since consultancies need packaged methods and boards want visible outcomes, and recommends asking whether a problem is a ball or a pigeon and running small experiments.
points: Treating an organisation as a machine is a category error, since complex adaptive systems cannot be steered by predicting the output of an input.
Big-bang change breaks the stable pattern that holds an organisation together while it adapts, and cannot choose what pattern replaces it.
The pandemic shift to remote work stuck because it imposed a constraint and left details to those doing the work, unlike transformation programmes that design details in advance.
Consultancies sell packaged methods and boards want visible results, which is why training courses and new structures beat slower work on how people actually interact.
The ball-or-pigeon question helps leaders decide when to plan with confidence and when to run small, cheap experiments and change constraints instead.
quotes: The fault often lies in the assumption that an organisation behaves like a machine, in which the right inputs produce predictable outputs. But organisations are complex adaptive systems, and managing one as if it were linear is a category error.
Fire a pigeon with the same force and every calculation is useless, because the pigeon responds to its surroundings and makes its own choices.
So a thoughtless remark from a leader can ripple through a department, while a meticulously planned restructure can fade into the unknown.
A big enough intervention can usually break that pattern. What it can’t do is choose the pattern that forms next..

The difference is that the pandemic imposed a new constraint and left the details to the people doing the work, whereas a transformation programme most often designs the details in advance and imposes them on everyone at once.
Consultancies that deliver transformation projects cannot easily scale if every engagement begins from scratch. They therefore seek methods that can be packaged, standardised, and priced in advance.
You can tell boards and teams plainly that nobody knows how a change will land, and mean it.
For example, payroll is a ball, and can be planned and delivered with confidence. Whether a new way of working takes hold is a pigeon, and no plan can promise it.
